title: I give up on Game Dev, it’s not for me
author: Saayaminator
selftext:
I wanted to do a TPS with RPG elements, and a hand painted/ cartoony style (inspired by The Bad Batch as you can see). Here was my process:  
\- Claude Code, Opus 5.5, for writing all code and doing passes on Blender  
\- Tripo P2 for all the low poly characters and props  
\- ElevenLabs for voices and music  
I let Opus access the APIs to make the assets and integrate them. I wrote my vision and planned the implementation. Took a while to get to a playable test level. Even then, I iterated many times on the gameplay, on the audio, on the animations, on the 3D models, …

This is what I learned in the end: This is not for me. The games I want to do have a big scope and I just don’t believe AI can fully get you there if you don’t know game development or spend a lot of time on it.

Even with AI assistance, it takes so long to learn all the aspects of game development. And it takes so long for all the little things to look right, the models, the music, the sound effects, the animations (god that was hard), the consistency, etc

TLDR: Skill issue and newfound respect for those who manage to create games, with or without AI support.

comments.author: J0rdian

replies.author: Connect_Scallion9184
replies.body:
I have a similar issue, but maybe to a lesser extent (I want to make large games, but the complexity is in the mechanics and not in the actual engine, like 3D, networks, etc.). My solution: pace yourself - take it as a marathon, not a sprint. If you do not need to find a source of income by yesterday, nothing stops you from taking a couple months longer or a year to do it.

What that gives you with AI-assisted games specifically is that even with full vibe-coding with minimal code knowledge, you can implement smaller chunks of stuff and control how the game plays and behaves (also test it). You will also learn a lot along the way.

At the end of the day if you dont want to do it - don't... but I wouldn't give up too fast :)

replies.author: askdoobie
replies.body:
It's even WAY harder and WAY worse than you think. Hold on to your butts:

I started learning programming from books when I was 14, using ActionScript and Flash. 

To make the music, I learned how to produce using Ableton and Cubase. I studied music theory, took keyboard lessons, learned mastering, and bought a professional sound card and monitor speakers. 

To make the art, I learned Photoshop and got myself a calibrated monitor. 

To make models and animations, I learned Cinema 4D from books and videos. I learned how to make keyframe animations. 

Then I studied a whole-ass computer science degree at a university. There, I learned several programming languages, at least four. 

I taught myself how to write game engines from scratch; I literally made my own physics engine, camera, shaders, and rendering from zero in fucking Python. 

Then I had to learn existing game engines, e.g., Unreal and Unity, and how they work. 

Then I landed a job as a AAA game programmer. The starting salary was 35k/year. The normal minimum starting salary was 45k. With what I knew, I could have easily applied to fucking NASA, yet they offer you the salary of a person working in a supermarket who has never learned anything. Gaming is a weird industry. People are passionate, which makes them good, and they would work almost for free. Besides that, gaming companies scout talent worldwide. It's normal to work in a team with people sitting in Spain, Poland, etc., so you're also competing with people living in cheaper areas (I'm in Germany).

If you don't do gaming for the lulz, don't do it.

replies.author: Flipf00t
replies.body:
I can attest to that! Started with an idea that by the time it was fleshed out would make even Rockstar/Bethesda quake at the thought of making it lol   
Doesn’t help that ai encouraged me.   
But after reading some Reddit communities, comments and tutorials on how to get the best out of your ai of choice, things have been a lot better. Games been slimed down to a far more reasonable scope, also considering the AI now knows my PC specs (cries in 750Ti). 

I’ve restarted hundreds of times but it’s how we learn, trial and error. Sure it’s taking me ages, but I’m having fun learning and trying things in the process. Just make sure anything you make, test, not use in the end - save in a separate folder - you never know when that might become useful again!

replies.author: JedahVoulThur
replies.body:
Exactly this. I'm on my fifth game and this is the first time I'm including enemies. My first game (in 2023) was a " player vs environment" where you have to gather scattered pieces, the second was a chatbot where it could be argued the AI was an enemy, I just used Player2, regex and a small Behavior Tree, the third one was a fishing game for a small 48hours jam, the fourth a point and click puzzle one.  
It's only with this fifth game that I am delving into the intricacies of creating a complex BT and balancing factions. Turn based RPGs are my favorite genre as a gamer and I was well aware I'd need lots of experience before trying to make one.  
I don't have a Claude subscription (I live in a third world country), I just use Arena.AI, Gemini through AIStudio and my own knowledge as I do know programming and have read a lot about design before even starting.

For OP and others in a similar situation. You definitely can reach the dream games you want to make, but only if you aren't anxious about it and have a little patience. Start small, practice with different projects the different areas. Recicle systems and components between projects and increase the complexity slowly.  
  
On the other hand, this thread reminded me of something. I've seen anti-ai people say that in the future nobody would share cultural experiences because everyone will just create their own media. I think that's bullshit, there will always be people that like to create things and people that don't, that just want to watch/play/read something. It doesn't matter how easy the creative process becomes, and that's completely fine.

replies.author: RevoIncubus
replies.body:
Give it, and yourself, time, if you really have the desire. Chase it - learn slowly, start small. 

I made all the same mistakes you did. Projects too big, too long, and not projects that played to my strengths. 

So I stopped, took a step back, and started again. I made a separate imprint just for testing small ideas and iterating on them. 

I’ve learned a ton just doing that. I’ve released a game on steam. Was huge failure, and that was okay by me. Because I learned so much about the process and what I was doing wrong. 

In the end, if you love it, you will be back. But, try approaching it from new directions. What you learn doing that might change your entire perspective on how this work and what your personal journey is going to be. In the end, it is an art form. Finding the way that feels right to you is a part of the journey.

comments.author: cratercamper
comments.body:
It looks very good. You can try to make the scope smaller, change the genre even (one multiplayer arena?, shooting puzzle?, turn based? ...).   
  
Or just keep it open - AI will be getting better, it will understand better and less effort will be required to do the bigger things. Lots of open source systems are appearing now and AI can use them.   
  
When you forget about the project for some months, the brain still works on it - it is unconscious, but inspiration is collected, solutions are sought ...and brilliant ideas might occur to you later.   
  
What is also fun with AI is creating the world and the story - sideline the implementation and dive into your fantasies - what world is that, what is there, why, how the conflict arose, what are the actors, what events/incidents/affairs happened, what people think there and how they are divided, maybe it can have some non-traditional elements, etc. If you build original world like that, you can then make the game rich with history, stories, situations. Or you can use the world in other game.

comments.author: New_Patience_8107
comments.body:
It's a full time job making a game even with the top models and following an SDLC. The more you make the more you're making prior steps redundant or cause tech debt and you have to go back and refactor so you've spent a whole day but barely see the effect on the other side.

Then you have those avalanche days where you break through something major. Then you go back to a week of fixing and fine tuning. That's what coding is. The one shot merchant's won't have the patience for this.

comments.author: Glum-Drop-5724
comments.body:
I am starting to feel the same. I am running a local agent (gyro s quant of qwen flash next) on a fairly low end system. I have managed to get it to make a basic tech demo of what I am envisioning. Its a 3D third person game in godot, I am not trying to get hyper realistic or high quality graphics, but its really hard getting things right still.

And the fact that I am using local AI means that I am not learning how things actually work, while the local AI agent is not good enough to fill the knowledge gaps I lack. I am slowly getting there, even such a simple thing as adding a bevel to the corners of a procedurally generated column seem to be difficult lmao. Yet at the same time I have managed to get pretty far. Might just be a skill issue combined with low end AI, and there is probably room for improvements with better prompts, better skills, mcps, feedback loops etc.

One thing I have learned is that game dev is really difficult and requires a ton of skills in many fields, both when it comes to coding, engineering, design, graphics, art, music, writing and so much more.

comments.author: -TimeMaster-
comments.body:
The only game I've really done was a 2D platform game that served as my wedding invitation. It was a game with only 5 levels, pretty quick to beat (20-45 minutes)

I spent 200 hours on it. 200.

I'm not primarily a developer although I know to code but I definitely didn't have any experience in game development.

I used free assets although I had to do additional work on some of them, specially the spritesheets for character animations.

I had to code everything by hand (it was early 2023), learn a new framework (phaser), learn how tilesheets and spritesheets work in order to build levels and manage animations, how a gaming loop works, and fix a lot of things I was encountering on my way.

No, game development is not easy. Shortcuts are almost never a good way to achieve things.

If you want something well done you'll need to put effort into it.

comments.author: zet23t
comments.body:
I am working 18 years in the industry and have experience in gamedev a couple more years on top.

Game dev is difficult for many reasons and you are experiencing it now. Playing a game and knowing it inside out is still a lot different from making the same game, because what players can not see is the lengthy journey of getting there. It is this experience that you are missing now: You know what the game should look and feel like, but you lack the map or even intuition of knowing how to get there or the ability to know what you can or can not do or what you should avoid doing. 

This has always been the case, but the results look way more impressive now.

What is worse about using AI from the beginning (in my opinion, there is not much experience around to know anything for sure): You miss out learning the important lessons the hard way. This is even a problem for veterans when trying to use AI on topics they lack experience with, even if they have more knowledge than someone starting from scratch.

I would still suggest not giving up. But try to approach it in a simpler fashion. Focus less on visuals. More on gameplay. Something I suck at, too. But I believe it is the right way to approach this.

comments.author: RamuneGaming
comments.body:
I think ambition is the biggest barrier to entry for game development. we all want to make great things from the get go "Wow I want to make a massive collectathon", "oh wouldn't it be cool if I make the next halo" but in reality you're more likely to release a smaller scoped game when being a solo dev, those bigger titles are made by massive teams who all have thier own dedicated roles and they barely overlap so they don't have to learn mutiple things such as artists doign art while audio engineers make audio etc. You then have a manager/producer/supervisor who does all the overlapping things like communicating between teams. Of course you do get the odd story of a single person doing like a massive FPS solo but in reality it likely took them like 5+ years if not more. Therefore, curbing that ambition is really what sets apart the experienced indie dev from the inexperienced one. Its where you need to start and by recognizing that it ok to work to a smaller scale that shows you're on your way to becoming experienced. But you know there is nothing wrong with not doing that too as with anything in life not everything is going to work for everyone we all have our own tastes and desires and that is fine.

I really like these down to earth honest posts and I hope you find your motivation again to continue this because honestly it does look pretty impressive, kinda gives me natural selection vibes. I could def see some parts being toned down to make the project overall more manageable.

Best of luck.
